hints: Look first at which hydrogen halide is made in each case, as concentrated sulfuric acid oxidises some halides but not others.
Notice that reaction 1 makes only $HCl$ fumes, which are too weak an oxidising agent to turn colourless $I^-$ into brown $I_2$.
For reaction 2, recall what normally happens with $Ag^+$ and $Cl^-$, then think how excess ammonia changes that by forming a soluble complex ion.
walkthrough:
**Identify the fumes in reaction 1**

Think of this as an acid-base reaction first. Chloride is not easily oxidised, so concentrated sulfuric acid just protonates it.

$$KCl + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow KHSO_4 + HCl$$
The fumes are $HCl$ gas.

**Test if HCl can oxidise iodide**

Bubbling $HCl$ into $KI(aq)$ would only give brown $I_2$ if $HCl$ could oxidise $I^-$. It cannot.

$$HCl + I^- \rightarrow \text{no reaction}$$
So the potassium iodide solution stays colourless. This rules out a brown solution.

**Recall the normal silver chloride test in reaction 2**

Normally, chloride and silver ions give a white precipitate.

$$Ag^+(aq) + Cl^-(aq) \rightarrow AgCl(s) \text{ white precipitate}$$
Students expect this here.

**Add the effect of aqueous ammonia**

Here the $Cl^-$ is already mixed with excess $NH_3$. Any $AgCl$ that tries to form immediately dissolves as the soluble diammine complex.

$$AgCl(s) + 2NH_3(aq) \rightarrow [Ag(NH_3)_2]^+(aq) + Cl^-(aq)$$
So no white precipitate is seen, only a colourless solution. Colourless plus colourless matches the correct row.

options.A: Incorrect. Brown solution for reaction 1 would mean $I_2$ formed. That happens with $HBr$ or $HI$, which are strong enough reducing agents to reduce concentrated $H_2SO_4$, but $HCl$ is not. Reaction 2 as colourless solution is correct, but reaction 1 is wrong.
options.B: Incorrect on both counts. It assumes $HCl$ oxidises $I^-$ to brown $I_2$, which it cannot, and it assumes normal $AgCl$ white precipitate forms, forgetting that excess $NH_3$ dissolves $AgCl$ as $[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+$. This is the double-trap choice.
options.C: Correct and well done. Reaction 1 stays colourless because $HCl$ cannot oxidise $I^-$. Reaction 2 stays colourless with no precipitate because excess ammonia keeps silver in solution as the soluble $[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+$ complex instead of white $AgCl$.
options.D: Half right, half wrong. Colourless solution for reaction 1 is correct, but white precipitate for reaction 2 ignores the ammonia. The key trick is that $AgCl$ is soluble in excess dilute ammonia, so no precipitate persists.
